How does a hundred-metre tree drink with no pump?
An ordinary suction pump can only lift water about ten metres.
Yet redwoods grow past a hundred and ten metres.
The trick starts at the top. Sun evaporates water from the leaves, and each lost molecule tugs on the next.
Thin tubes called xylem hold unbroken threads of water, down to the roots.
So the water isn't pushed. It's pulled, under negative pressure. Literally stretched.
In 1965, scientists measured it: about minus five atmospheres in damp forests, minus eighty in deserts.
In 2008, engineers built a gel synthetic tree that pulls water the same way.
But stretched water is fragile. In severe drought, air bubbles snap the threads, and trees can die.
Every tree you pass is lifting stretched water, pulled by the sun.
